summary:
TANGO: Dancing with SARs is a website for exploring data from the NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar (NISAR) mission. Users can explore a 3D globe, visit locations around the world, and look at environmental changes in real satellite observations. The site offers before-and-after radar comparisons, visualizations, and statistical analysis for events like flooding, vegetation change, and coastal erosion. In some places, we also use imagery from other satellites. Each case walks users through what changed, what the evidence shows, and how uncertain the conclusions are.

Radar data is hard for non-specialists to read. TANGO pairs real NASA data with plain-language explanations so more people can use it.
details:
TANGO: Dancing with SARs

Overview

TANGO is a website to explore data from the NASA-ISRO Synthetical Aperture Radar mission. Radar can penetrate clouds and darkness to monitor changes in the Earth’s environment. However, this typically requires specific software and knowledge. TANGO lets students, researchers, and curious individuals have a look at the data for themselves using an interactive globe.

How it works

Users navigate around a 3D globe, created using CesiumJS, to select different locations in the world such as the Florida Everglades, Louisiana Delta, California, Hawaii, Alaska, and Namibia. At each location, users will complete an investigation into the satellite observations. They will be able to compare data against a chosen date, see what measurements were taken, and discover what this data may show.

Every investigation asks four questions:

  1. What did the satellite observe?
  2. What changed between observations?
  3. What could explain the difference?
  4. How reliable is the evidence?

This ensures that even if there seems to be a big difference between two sets of data, we ensure users have considered everything.

Processing NASA Data

All results are based on real data from NISAR. A Python pipeline has been created to process data from NISAR Level-2 Geocoded Polarimetric Covariance products (GCOV) obtained from NASA Earthdata and Alaska Satellite Facility. The pipeline processes HH and HV polarisations to create quicklooks and statistical summaries from valid source products.

Once processed, users will be able to compare radar backscatter, pixel distribution, and selected areas. There are quality checks and data sources to ensure users understand the difference between the measurements and what may have caused it.

Tools

Python was used to access and process the data. Next.js, React, and TypeScript were used to create the website. CesiumJS and MapLibre were used to create the globe and perform geospatial comparison. GitHub was used for collaboration, and Vercel was used to deploy the website. Claude Code and Codex were used to aid coding.

What sets it apart

Users have a familiar interface with a globe, meaning they do not need knowledge of radar file types. The main features are:

  • Interactive 3D globe exploration across diverse global environments.
  • Before-and-after satellite comparisons with swipe, side-by-side, and difference views.
  • Real HH/HV statistical analysis and histograms for processed NISAR locations.
  • Regional analysis that allows users to examine selected areas more closely.
  • Location-specific explanations of environmental processes.
  • Transparent scientific quality checks, limitations, and source information.
  • Educational resources explaining radar measurements and common interpretation mistakes.

We have a specific FAQ page to help users understand how to interpret the satellite measurements.

Overall, this means TANGO has become more than a simple image viewer. It is a tool for users to explore scientific observations and learn how evidence can support conclusions.

Challenges We Faced

One of our biggest technical challenges was handling NISAR's GCOV validity masks correctly. Unlike a simple binary mask, the GCOV mask uses values from 1–254 to identify valid subswaths, while 0 and 255 indicate invalid or out-of-acquisition pixels. Treating every nonzero value as invalid would incorrectly discard legitimate radar measurements. Our pipeline distinguishes these mask values, excludes nonfinite and nonpositive radar power, and processes valid pixels before generating comparisons.

We also had to account for how radar measurements are converted into decibels. Because the source data represents linear radar power, our pipeline averages valid power before applying 10·log10 during spatial reduction, rather than averaging logarithmic values directly. We aligned observations to common grids and distinguished differences between separately calculated medians from actual pixel-by-pixel changes.

Another challenge was explaining the results. Radar backscatter can change because of surface moisture, roughness, vegetation, speckle, or observation conditions. We therefore designed each investigation to separate what was measured from what it might mean, while making unresolved scientific limitations visible.

Intended Impact

TANGO was created for students, those without a background in remote sensing, and anyone curious about how NISAR satellite imagery can help us better understand our changing planet. Users can explore observations from environments where flooding, coastal erosion, vegetation changes, and volcanic activity are studied. They can also practice questioning what they see and evaluating how reliable the evidence is.

We hope to demonstrate to more people what NASA's Earth observation missions can offer. We have not yet conducted formal user testing, so measuring how effectively TANGO improves understanding is an important next step.

What's Next

At the moment, TANGO is heavily based on investigations prepared by our team. Not all changes in radar data can be fully explained by the measurements themselves. We hope to improve our Coordinate Explorer so users can reliably create investigations for their own locations, rather than relying on our preset examples.

We also plan to add longer time series and additional independent environmental data so we can provide more comprehensive explanations of what changed, why it may have changed, and how this information could benefit real-world research and education.
